During Ramchandra Ray’s escape, Sitaram enforces the order against leaving, and Udayaditya responds by disarming and binding him. During Udayaditya’s own escape from prison, Sitaram opens his cell and leads him out, reversing their dynamic: the guard who obstructed the prince becomes the prince’s rescuer.

Pratapaditya first ordered two Pathan men to kill Basanta Ray at the inn in Simultali while he traveled to Jessore, but that plan failed. Finally, he sent Muktiyar Khan and soldiers, disguised in plain clothes and entering Raigarh through different gates, to execute a signed death warrant; after praying and blessing Pratapaditya, Basanta Ray was killed by Abdul with a drawn sword.

1. In the Mahishi’s room in Jessore’s inner quarters, disguised as a middle-aged woman called “Mother Nikasha.”
2. In the king’s chamber in Chandradwip’s palace, disguised as a jester.
Surma takes the poison secretly prepared by Mangala and dies before the planned exile can take place.

Ramchandra Ray takes Vibha’s refusal as a grave insult and retaliates by marrying another woman. When Vibha later arrives, she learns that her husband no longer wants her, shattering her hopes of reunion and leaving her heartbroken.

After Rukmini takes the ring from Udayaditya, Sitaram and Bhagavat use its seal bearing the Yubaraj’s name to stamp a forged petition falsely accusing Udayaditya of plotting with the Emperor to seize Pratapaditya’s kingdom. Bhagavat presents the petition to Pratapaditya as one he intercepted from Udayaditya’s fleeing servant, supposedly bound for Delhi. The genuine signet makes the forgery appear authentic, and the alleged conspiracy serves as justification for Udayaditya’s imprisonment, despite Pratapaditya’s private doubts about its credibility.

Ramchandra Ray’s escape is followed by the dismissal of palace guards, prompting Udayaditya to provide them and their families with financial support. Surma secretly arranges the stipends through a trusted maid, but the scheme is exposed because the maid fails to keep it secret from Mangala. When Pratapaditya learns of the payments, he is enraged at Udayaditya’s defiance of his prohibition and retaliates by ordering Surma to her paternal home, separating her from Udayaditya as a punishment.

The song expresses Basanta Ray’s loneliness, grief, and sense of abandonment: those he loved are gone, leaving only emptiness and no joy in singing or living. He first hums it alone at sunset on his veranda in Raigarh, quietly longing for his loved ones and wondering whether he will see them again. Later, in Jessore, overwhelmed by his family’s desolation, he sings it heartbrokenly while holding Vibha’s hand in the silent, empty room that once echoed with joy.

Rukmini’s failed attack allowed Udayaditya to escape. She then reported the escape to Pratapaditya, accused Basanta Ray and Sitaram, and helped the soldiers capture Udayaditya at Raigarh. Pratapaditya had sent Muktiyar Khan with an order to kill Basanta Ray if Udayaditya could not be found; Muktiyar carried out the death sentence despite Udayaditya’s offer to surrender.

Pratapaditya initially receives Ramchandra coldly and without ceremony: there is no musical welcome, the escort is inadequate, the elephant is smaller than expected, and he dismisses Ramchandra after a perfunctory audience, leaving Ramchandra bowing deferentially and realizing Pratapaditya’s superiority. Later, Ramchandra reverses this deference by joining daily court ridicule of Pratapaditya as a low-born upstart, insulting his lineage, and boasting that marrying his daughter has redeemed his own dynasty’s seven generations and that Pratapaditya’s family is beneath his court.

Rukmini returns under the name Mangala, living on the outskirts of Jessore as a practitioner of tantra, mantras, and medicine. She befriends the palace servants, keeps track of palace affairs, and learns of the growing hostility toward Surma. When the Rajmahishi decides to send Surma away, wanting Udayaditya’s affection returned to her first, Matangini secretly obtains Mangala’s medicine. Mangala spends five days preparing slow-acting poison, treating it with rituals meant to remove any pity for Surma. Surma takes the poison and dies, with the palace believing she has killed herself. Rukmini then pursues her ambition further, conspiring with Sitaram and later entering Udayaditya’s chamber, invoking his guilt toward her, demanding his love, and taking his ring so that her mantra can work toward her dream of ruling him and Jessore.

Udayaditya’s early lament grows into a firm conviction that he is unfit to rule. Constant scrutiny, neglect, and contempt follow his failure as administrator, while his royal status also brings humiliation to Surma. He begins to dream of abandoning the court and living as an ordinary man. After a catastrophe that leads to his grand-uncle’s death, he blames his own weakness and believes he has ruined the lives of those who hoped in him. Facing his father, Pratapaditya, he declares himself unworthy and asks for release from the throne, acknowledging Samaraditya as the heir. He then makes the renunciation formal: before his father in the temple, he swears on Ma-Kali that he will never claim any part of Jessore’s territory, sit on its throne, or touch its royal scepter, accepting responsibility for his grand-uncle’s murder if he ever breaks the oath. He leaves for Kashi to live as an ascetic.

Ramchandra gave the letter to Nayanchand to deliver to Pratapaditya, but Nayanchand, fearing its consequences, diverted it to the Mahishi. She kept it from both Pratapaditya and Vibha and showed it to Basanta Ray, who interpreted it as Ramchandra requesting Vibha’s return to Chandradwip. Following his advice, the Mahishi announced to Vibha and the household that her husband had asked for her to be sent back, and Vibha gratefully believed that he understood and forgiven her.

Although Pratapaditya had the palace canal blocked with large salwood logs, Rammohan and his followers pulled the boat up and over them. The guards’ stones could not reach the fleeing boat, and their gun was useless without a flintlock, gunpowder, or bullets. After further delays in arranging a chase boat, they discovered that the fugitives had already escaped beyond capture.

Basanta Ray’s sitar, once his “eternal companion” and a source of shared music and joy, becomes a symbol of his separation from Udayaditya. At their farewell, he leaves it behind and vows never to play it again; later, he describes its strings as broken and unable to be tuned, mirroring his own broken heart and the emptiness left by his loved ones’ absence. The silence of his once-cherished instrument reflects the despair that deepens when he hears that Udayaditya is imprisoned, leaving him overwhelmed and helplessly crying, “Dada, come to me!”

Earlier, Udayaditya was known for courageously intervening on behalf of oppressed subjects, protecting them without hesitation or concern for the consequences. After Surma’s death, he became so dominated by fear of Pratapaditya that he could no longer act: he turned away from a beaten subject, abandoned plans to stop a planned plunder, and no longer dared to provide financial help. His former courage had given way to fear, hesitation, and inaction.
Sitaram rescues Udayaditya from the prison caused by their conspiracy: when the prison catches fire, he warns Udayaditya, pulls him out, and leads him away.

First, he carries Ramchandra Ray on his back down a rope made from twisted sheets, anchoring it to a palace roof pillar and lowering the king carefully into a waiting boat. Later, after the king insults Vibha and she faints, Rammohan lifts her, places her in a palanquin, and takes her out of the palace to the boat.

In Jessore, Vibha is dressed as a lavishly adorned, joyful bride, wearing eight thick gold bangles and a huge diamond bracelet on each arm, a large nose ring, and an elaborate hairstyle, though the heavy adornments leave her flustered. In Chandradwip, she deliberately appears as a common woman—a beggar—in a plain veil, entering the palace unrecognized and treated like a maidservant. Her presentation shifts from shy, radiant anticipation to mortified despair, trembling and fainting.

In his bedchamber, the window symbolizes lingering hope and the possibility of Surma’s return: he sits where she used to sit, gazes at the unchanged moonlight and garden, and imagines hearing her voice. In the prison, it becomes a symbol of freedom and release. Through the small window, he sees the sky and birds and imagines his cage breaking and his spirit swimming freely through that endless sky. Since the soft bed in the palace is his real prison, the window keeps alive his conviction that, despite his confinement, his inner freedom remains intact and his release will eventually come.

Sitaram first approaches Rukmini because he is penniless but strongly attracted to her beauty and money. She lends him cash without demanding an immediate repayment, and he interprets her performance of affection as encouragement. He responds with romantic declarations, flirtatious jokes—even about interest—and repeated visits, while his promise to repay disappears. Their arrangement thus becomes one in which he enjoys her money and attention while avoiding repayment, and she tolerates his presumption.

When the Yubaraj is imprisoned, their flirtation turns to open hostility. Sitaram curses Rukmini and threatens to kill her; she responds with hatred and a jealous assertion that the Yubaraj belongs to her and that only she can help or harm him. After helping engineer the Yubaraj’s escape and covering it with a fire, Sitaram goes to Rukmini’s house intending to rob her, assuming she is dead. Instead, he finds her wet, disheveled, and seemingly returned from Yama’s door. She vows to put both Sitaram and the Yubaraj into the oven and then die. When he tries to pacify her with feigned affection, she becomes more enraged, fetches a curved blade, and attacks the place where he stood; he barely escapes. She then exposes Sitaram’s conspiracy to King Pratapaditya and has men sent after the fugitives. What begins as an opportunistic, money-backed flirtation ends in mutual death threats, a desperate attempted reconciliation, and Rukmini actively pursuing Sitaram as her enemy.

Sitaram began by creating a controlled emergency: with the help of loyal commoners and palace servants, he set several guardhouse rooms alight, while some of his men sabotaged firefighting by wasting water, failing to return with it, smashing pots, and creating confusion. Amid the chaos, he told Udayaditya that the prison was burning and led him out, eventually putting him on a boat.

The plan then became a systematic cover-up. Sitaram returned with Udayaditya’s sword, and his men set fire to the empty prison cell and placed bones, a skull, and the sword inside to suggest that his body had been destroyed. False reports of Udayaditya’s screams, the cell’s collapsed roof, and his lack of response reinforced the supposed death. The guards then argued and blamed one another instead of immediately investigating an escape. Sitaram also recovered the prince’s letters, which he had prevented from reaching the palace, and destroyed all but those intended for the Mahishi and Vibha. Thus, the original diversion became a staged disappearance supported by planted evidence, manipulated witnesses, and destruction of potentially incriminating correspondence. The deception later collapsed when Rukmini exposed Sitaram’s role to Pratapaditya.

Ramchandra Ray dismisses the rescue as an act motivated by Udayaditya’s concern for his sister, not for Ramchandra himself, and shows no gratitude, instead joining his courtiers in mocking and ridiculing Udayaditya as Pratapaditya’s son.

Although Pratapaditya scornfully dismisses the Emperor of Delhi’s anger and assumes that no complaint could be lodged against him, others exploit Delhi’s power for their own ends. Resenting Pratapaditya and wanting Udayaditya to rule, Bhagavat and Sitaram forge a petition bearing the prince’s seal, accusing him of plotting to seize the kingdom. Bhagavat then brings the petition secretly to Pratapaditya instead of the Emperor, concealing Sitaram’s involvement. Believing his son genuinely guilty, Pratapaditya resolves to punish him. Thus, the specter of Delhi—first dismissed as an empty threat—becomes the pretext for his son’s confinement through a scheme engineered not by the Emperor, but by the prince’s own would-be supporters.

Surma’s presence is marked by her tenderness toward Vibha: Vibha secretly has her hair styled to her own liking, only to have the Mahishi undo and restyle it. After Surma is gone, hair-grooming becomes an emblem of loss. Vibha waits quietly for Surma to braid her hair, but evening falls and her hair remains unbraided. Later, Rammohan finds it unkempt and recognizes that no one is caring for her. Braided hair recalls Surma’s intimate, reassuring care, while unbraided, unkempt hair expresses Vibha’s grief and the emptiness left in the palace.
